stemMd: Which of the following is best supported by the passage?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The lower working hours found in diaries may partly reflect who agrees to keep a diary, and not only more careful measurement.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Questionnaires should no longer be used to measure how people spend their time.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Employers' records are more accurate than either diaries or questionnaires.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The working week has become longer in recent decades.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Most employed adults deliberately exaggerate their working hours when answering questionnaires.

explanationMd:
The best-supported choice is one you can build from statements in the text, hedged no further than they allow. The third paragraph says the people who volunteer to keep diaries "tend to be those with a little spare time", and that public debate compares "a figure from one kind of instrument with a figure from the other". A diary-based figure for working hours is drawn from those volunteers, so it can come out low partly because people with spare time tend to work less, not only because diaries measure more carefully.

A sharp reader will object that the second paragraph compares diaries with questionnaires answered by the same people, so self-selection cannot explain that within-person gap. That is right, and it is why the choice says "may partly" and "not only": it grants that careful measurement is part of the story, as the same-person comparison shows, and adds only that who keeps a diary can also pull diary figures down when they are used as estimates for a whole population. The choice would overreach if it said selection explained all of the gap; it does not.

The other choices fail more plainly. Deliberate exaggeration is ruled out by the first paragraph ("not usually dishonesty"). Abandoning questionnaires ignores the stated trade-off between depth and coverage. Ranking employers' records above both instruments goes beyond the text, which never assesses those records. A longer working week is exactly the question the passage says debate has handled badly, and it gives no evidence either way.

distractorRationale.e: The first paragraph says the gap is "not usually dishonesty" but a matter of how people summarise a week, so deliberate exaggeration by most adults is contradicted.
distractorRationale.b: The third paragraph presents a trade-off between depth and coverage in which questionnaires reach many people; the passage calls the lesson "modest" and never recommends dropping them.
distractorRationale.d: The passage mentions the debate about the length of the working week only to say it mixes figures from different instruments. It gives no evidence on which way the week has moved.
distractorRationale.c: Employers' records are mentioned only as a benchmark against which questionnaire answers look high. The passage never compares them with diaries or ranks the three sources.

accessibilityText: An inference question about the time diaries passage. It asks which statement is best supported by the passage. The five choices: the lower working hours found in diaries may partly reflect who agrees to keep a diary, and not only more careful measurement; questionnaires should no longer be used to measure how people spend their time; employers' records are more accurate than either diaries or questionnaires; the working week has become longer in recent decades; most employed adults deliberately exaggerate their working hours on questionnaires.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original passage. Every option is answerable, or refutable, from the passage text alone.

review.author: tolc-e-wave6-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Paragraph 3 says diary volunteers tend to be people with a little spare time, so the lower diary hours may partly reflect who takes part rather than only more careful measurement. B overreaches, since the passage recommends a trade-off, not dropping questionnaires. C is never claimed. D is only a public debate the passage treats with caution. E contradicts 'The gap is not usually dishonesty'. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tolce-verbal-run2) reached the same answer: Paragraph 3 says the people who volunteer for diaries 'tend to be those with a little spare time', so lower diary hours may partly reflect who takes part, which is the hedged claim in A. B is too strong, since the passage calls for a trade-off, not for dropping questionnaires. C is never claimed: records are only said to be lower than questionnaire answers. D is the unresolved debate, and E contradicts 'The gap is not usually dishonesty'.]

review.notes: Uniqueness check: the correct choice combines two stated facts (lower diary hours; volunteers have spare time) and is hedged. Each other choice contradicts the text or goes beyond it. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
